title: How to Successfully Appeal an Insurance Denial in Texas
description: Learn how to successfully appeal an insurance denial on a Galveston property or TWIA claim: read the letter, gather proof, meet deadlines and ask for help.
keyword: how to successfully appeal an insurance denial
html:
A denial letter feels final, but it usually is not. Insurers deny property claims for many reasons, and some of those reasons can be answered with better evidence, a closer reading of the policy, or a correction of the facts. This guide explains how to successfully appeal an insurance denial on a Galveston home or business, including windstorm claims handled by the Texas Windstorm Insurance Association (TWIA).

No one can promise a denial will be reversed. What you can do is make sure the insurer has every relevant fact in front of it, in writing, before its decision stands. That is what a strong appeal does.

Step 1: Read the Denial Letter Line by Line

Start with the letter itself. A denial should explain the reason and point to the policy language the insurer is relying on. Highlight three things:

  • The stated reason. Common examples: damage is wear and tear, damage pre-existed the storm, the cause was flood rather than wind, the loss was reported late, or the damage is below the deductible.
  • The policy provisions cited. Write down every section, exclusion or endorsement named.
  • Any deadlines or next steps. Some letters describe a reconsideration process, appraisal, or other dispute options, and some of these have their own time limits.

If the letter is vague, ask the insurer in writing to identify the specific policy language and the facts it relied on. You are entitled to understand why you were denied.

Step 2: Get the Full Claim File and Your Complete Policy

You cannot answer a denial without seeing what the adjuster saw. Request in writing:

  • A certified copy of your full policy, including every endorsement.
  • The adjuster's inspection photos and field notes.
  • Any engineer's or expert's report used in the decision.
  • The insurer's estimate, if one was prepared.

Engineering reports deserve close attention on coastal wind claims. Check the date of inspection, how long the inspector was on site, which areas were actually examined, and whether the conclusions match your photos.

Step 3: Match the Evidence to the Reason for Denial

Knowing how to successfully appeal an insurance denial really comes down to this step. Your appeal should respond directly to the stated reason, not simply repeat that you disagree. Some examples:

  • Wear and tear or pre-existing damage: provide dated photos of the property before the storm (real estate listings, old phone photos, prior inspection reports) and a roofer or contractor's written opinion on the age and pattern of the damage.
  • Wind vs. flood: document the water line, where damage appears above it, and wind-driven damage such as missing shingles, lifted flashing or broken windows. Our shingle wind damage calculator shows how different shingle ratings respond at different wind speeds, which can help frame the discussion.
  • Storm did not reach damaging speeds at your address: gather local weather data for the date of loss. Our Galveston weather events log tracks high-wind events for the area.
  • Late notice: explain when you discovered the damage and why, with any supporting facts.
  • Below deductible: get an independent, line-item estimate. Initial estimates sometimes miss interior water damage, underlayment, flashing, gutters or code-required items.

Special Rules for TWIA Denials

If your windstorm policy is through TWIA, the process is governed by Chapter 2210 of the Texas Insurance Code, and it has its own timelines and dispute steps that differ from a standard homeowners claim. A few key points:

  • TWIA claims must be reported within one year of the date of loss. If you have not filed yet, do not wait.
  • TWIA's decision letters explain your dispute options and the deadlines attached to them. Read those instructions carefully and calendar every date.
  • Because the TWIA process is structured and deadline driven, many policyholders choose to get professional help early rather than after a deadline has passed.

Our TWIA claims expert page walks through the TWIA process in more detail, and our Texas windstorm rules page covers the windstorm certification and inspection rules that often come up in coastal denials.

If you are unsure how to successfully appeal an insurance denial for your specific reason, ask a contractor, engineer or public adjuster which evidence would carry the most weight before you write anything.

Step 4: Write a Clear, Organized Appeal

A good appeal letter is short, factual and easy for a reviewer to follow. Include:

  1. Your name, property address, policy number, claim number and date of loss.
  2. A one-paragraph summary of what happened and what you are asking for.
  3. The insurer's stated reason for denial, quoted exactly.
  4. Your response to each reason, with evidence referenced by exhibit number.
  5. A list of attached exhibits: photos, estimates, expert opinions, weather data, receipts.
  6. A request for a written response and a reasonable date by which you expect it.

Send it in a way you can prove, such as certified mail or email with a read receipt, and keep a complete copy.

Step 5: Ask for a Re-Inspection

If the original inspection was brief or missed areas, ask for a re-inspection and be present for it. Walk the adjuster to every damaged area, including the attic, interior ceilings and any exterior elevations they did not examine. If you have a contractor or public adjuster, ask them to attend as well.

Step 6: Know Your Other Options

If a reconsideration does not resolve the dispute, other paths may be available depending on your policy and the type of disagreement:

  • Appraisal: many property policies include an appraisal clause for disagreements about the amount of loss. It generally does not decide coverage questions.
  • Complaint to TDI: the Texas Department of Insurance accepts consumer complaints about insurers and can ask the company to respond.
  • Legal advice: for coverage disputes, bad faith concerns or approaching deadlines, speak with a Texas attorney who handles insurance matters. Public adjusters cannot give legal advice.

Texas also sets claim-handling deadlines for insurers through the Prompt Payment of Claims Act, Chapter 542 of the Insurance Code. If your insurer is not responding, document every delay.

How a Public Adjuster Helps Appeal a Denial

A licensed public adjuster represents you, not the insurer. Texas public adjusters are licensed by TDI. On a denied claim, a public adjuster can re-inspect the property, build a detailed estimate, gather the evidence that answers the denial reason, and present the claim to the carrier. For many homeowners, understanding how to successfully appeal an insurance denial is less about knowing the steps and more about having the time and expertise to carry them out while also managing repairs and daily life.

Quick Appeal Checklist

  • Denial letter read and reasons highlighted
  • Full policy and claim file requested in writing
  • Deadlines on the letter calendared
  • Evidence gathered for each denial reason
  • Independent estimate obtained
  • Appeal letter sent with exhibits and proof of delivery
  • Re-inspection requested
  • Next options (appraisal, TDI complaint, attorney) identified

faq.q: Can a denied insurance claim be reopened?
faq.a: Often, yes. Many insurers will reconsider a denial when you provide new information, such as additional photos, an independent estimate or an expert opinion that addresses the stated reason. Put your request in writing and keep proof of delivery.

faq.q: What is the deadline to report a TWIA claim?
faq.a: TWIA claims must be reported within one year of the date of loss. After a claim decision, TWIA's letters describe additional dispute options and their own deadlines, so read each letter carefully and calendar every date.

faq.q: Should I hire a public adjuster or an attorney for a denied claim?
faq.a: It depends on the dispute. A public adjuster, licensed by TDI, can document damage and present the claim. Coverage disputes, bad faith concerns or lawsuit deadlines call for a Texas attorney. Some claims benefit from both.
